newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Golan settlers say Syria does not want peace.
newsitem.headline: Golan settlers say Syria does not want peace.

text.p: Doves or hawks, Israelis on the occupied Golan Heights say Syrian President Hafez al-Assad does not want peace with the Jewish state.
If he did, they say, the strategic plateau where 16,000 Israelis have put down roots since their country captured it in the 1967 Middle East war, would now be under Damascus's control.

The Golan residents say they could see even Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who with his Likud party ousted the Labour-led government in May elections on a platform opposed to trading land for peace, compromising on the Golan.
If Assad only really wanted peace.

"He could have got the Golan back long ago...He didn't because he has a different way of thinking," Avi Zeira, 45, head of the Golan Residents Committee, spearhead of the fight to keep Israel on the Golan under any circumstances, said at a well-appointed office in the region's main town, Katzrin.

Yigal Kipnis, 47, who founded a group that publicly backed the previous government's four-year drive to achieve a land-for-peace formula that might have booted him from the farming community of Maale Gamle, said Zeira was right, so far.
"I certainly agree that the key to results of the negotiations is with the Syrians," Kipnis said.
What divides the two men, and Israel, is whether Assad can change his tune and give Israel the security guarantees and full peace necessary for any Golan compromise.

And, if Assad did agree, whether such an agreement would be worth the risk of handing him the heights that tower hundreds of metres (yards) above northern Israel and from which Syrian gunners periodically shelled Israel before the 1967 war.

Pollster Hanoch Smith last conducted a survey on the issue of trading the Golan for peace with Syria before the elections. Smith found 54 percent of Israelis opposed to any compromise, 36 percent backed some compromise, and 10 percent undecided.

On the heights, a traditional Labour stronghold, Zeira said 68 percent voted for parties now in the government coalition. In the direct election for prime minister, 54 percent voted for Netanyahu and 46 percent for former prime minister Shimon Peres.
In 1992, before direct election of prime minister, about 60 percent of the Golan voted for the Labour party.

Both Zeira and Kipnis fought on the windswept plateau in the 1973 Middle East war, when Syria on the Golan and Egypt in the Sinai launched a surprise attack on the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur.

Both have invested their lives in developing the Golan, which in many ways still looks like a theatre of war. Israel's military presence is overwhelming. There seem to be more rough military camps than well-groomed civilian communities.

Here and there along roads through pastoral scenes helicopters suddenly clatter overhead; tanks queuing for manoeuvres chew up fallow fields. On the horizon, the tops of extinct volcanoes bristle with sophisticated listening systems.
There are war's ruins: flattened concrete Syrian bunkers and basalt stone villages abandoned 29 years ago dot the landscape.
In 1974, Israel and Syria cut a disengagement agreement. Since then, not a shot has been fired along the border.
Zeira, who not only fought but lost a brother in the war on the heights, says it would be madness to change the situation.
"We see that Syria has no real peace with any of its neighbours...and at the same time, tomorrow Assad might decide to be an ally of (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein," he said.
"Deterence is the most important element in the region and we have to keep it this way."
Sixty kms (40 miles) from the occupied heights, Damascus is within sight -- and rolling distance -- of Israel's army.
In addition, water sources on the Golan provide 30 percent of parched Israel's needs.
Zeira said continuing negotiations was important to prevent war, not necessarily to achieve peace -- because "real and full peace...is not natural in this region".
Talks have yet to resume under Netanyahu.
In the meantime, Zeira said the Golan would develop. Plans to build 2,000 more housing units should be in order soon, he said, and he expected work to begin in three months.
Kipnis said true peace, with the stringent security guarantees the late Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin sought and Damascus rejected, was the best strategic asset of all.

What no one should be prepared to accept, he said, was another war over land that in the end would be given up as happened with the Sinai. Under a 1979 peace treaty with Egypt, Israel gave back the entire peninsula captured in 1967.
But the first question, Kipnis said, was: Did Syria want peace? Was it ready to salve the Jewish state's security fears?
"If it is possible to reach an agreement, a Likud government will also reach an agreement, the same agreement, not better than the Labour party would have reached," Kipnis said.
Zeira agreed Likud, which he trusted in the main, might cut a deal -- if pressured.
"It can happen in the Likud government if, God forbid, there will be some changes in the policy of the United States, if there will be a threat from the U.S. establishment," he said.
Zeira said after the prior government's willingness to compromise, no Israeli could take for granted life on the 1,158 sq km (452 sq mile) Golan, also home to 18,000 Syrian Druze.
"We believe that from now on we shall have to live with this uncertainty and with this struggle. Maybe forever," he said.
